Our study investigates the evolution of Java dependency bloat in open-source projects from 2015 to 2020. Contrary to expectations, we found that project growth does not necessarily lead to an increase in unnecessary code. We discovered that projects with larger codebases are more prone to having excessive dependencies, and this trend is more pronounced in rapidly expanding projects. Our findings also indicate that projects with active maintenance tend to have fewer unnecessary dependencies. To address the issue of bloated dependencies, we propose a simple method to identify and remove unneeded transitive dependencies, and we demonstrate its effectiveness in improving project efficiency.

The synthesis of complex molecular structures is a crucial aspect of modern chemistry, particularly in the pharmaceutical industry. Advances in synthetic chemistry have led to the development of innovative methods for creating intricate organic compounds. This research focuses on a novel approach to synthesizing complex molecules using entangled photons. By entangling two photons, scientists can control the outcome of chemical reactions and create a wide range of molecular structures. This study explores the use of biphoton entanglement in chemical synthesis and its potential applications in the pharmaceutical industry. The findings suggest that this technique could be a valuable tool for chemists in the pursuit of new drugs and pharmaceutical compounds.

A novel method for determining the optimal solution in multistage distributionally robust optimization problems is proposed. This new approach, based on the concept of effective scenarios, offers a more efficient way to calculate the optimal solution compared to existing methods. By leveraging the total variation distance, effective scenarios are identified as a subset of the original scenarios that yield the same result as the original optimization problem. A detailed mathematical formulation of this approach is provided, along with a proof of its validity. Furthermore, the proposed method is demonstrated to be more efficient than existing methods by reducing the computational complexity of the optimization problem. A numerical example is also provided to illustrate the effectiveness of this approach.

Action anticipation in human motion is a crucial component in various applications, including sports analysis and human-robot interaction. This research proposes a novel approach to action anticipation that leverages a hybrid model combining a recurrent neural network (RNN) and radial basis function (RBF) kernel. The proposed model, referred to as RBF-RNN, utilizes the RNN component to capture temporal dependencies in action sequences and the radial basis function kernel to model the local geometric structure of the data. The model's performance is evaluated on two public datasets, Human3.6M and Ego4D, and the results demonstrate its superiority over existing methods. The code for this approach is available at https://github.com/Chao-Wang-USTC/RBF-RNN.

We introduce a solvable model of a quantum many-body system that undergoes thermalization through a process of repeated, periodic interactions. The interactions are governed by a time-dependent parameter that is controlled by an external clock. The system's behavior is analyzed in the context of a classical stochastic process, with the results showing that the system reaches thermal equilibrium at a rate determined by the time it takes for the interactions to occur. The model's predictions are validated through numerical simulations of a quantum spin chain, with the results indicating that the time it takes for the system to reach thermal equilibrium is proportional to the time it takes for the interactions to occur. The model's findings provide new insights into the dynamics of quantum systems that are subject to periodic interactions, with the potential for applications in the study of quantum computing and quantum information processing.

We establish a symbol class on the product of a homogeneous tree, defined by a Dr\"{a}gunc-Russell distance, and show that associated operators with symbols in this class are bounded from L^p(T) to L^q(T) for a specific range of p and q values. Furthermore, we introduce a new class of symbols, resulting in operators with specific properties, namely that they map from L^1(T) to L^1(T) in a compact and nuclear manner.

This research paper delves into the key aspects of 5G wireless technology, particularly focusing on the development of 5G mobile networks and the anticipated effects of 5G smartphones. A comprehensive analysis of 5G network design is presented, along with a discussion on the anticipated emergence of 5G smartphones and their influence on network infrastructure.

Deep learning models often exhibit overconfidence when encountering data outside their distribution, which can be particularly problematic in safety-critical applications. To address this issue, we introduce Chamfer Out-of-Distribution examples (CODEs), a novel approach to generating OOD samples that capture the full range of potential OOD data. By utilizing a Chamfer distance-based metric, our method creates a diverse set of samples that can be used to train more robust models capable of accurately identifying OOD data. Our approach is evaluated on a variety of image classification and segmentation tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in producing OOD samples that outperform existing methods in out-of-distribution detection.

The CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider measured the angular relationships between specific jet groups in proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy. The study focused on inclusive 2-jet, 3-jet, and 4-jet events, with each event's properties measured and recorded. The data, collected with a 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ luminosity, was used to calculate the average transverse momentum of the jets and the angle between them. The analysis found that the average angle between the jets was consistent with theoretical predictions from the next-to-leading order of QCD theory. The data was also used to calculate the average angle between the jets in 3-jet and 4-jet events, with the results being compared to theoretical predictions from the next-to-leading order of QCD theory. The analysis found that the average angle between the jets was consistent with the theoretical predictions, with the results being within the expected range of uncertainty.

Deep learning has revolutionized computer vision, with numerous breakthroughs achieved in tasks such as object detection, segmentation, and pose estimation. The success of these advancements can be attributed to the development of semi-supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, which enable the training of deep models using limited or no labeled data. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of semi-supervised and unsupervised learning methods in deep visual learning, focusing on recent advancements in object classification, image retrieval, and object detection. It also explores the challenges and future directions of this field, which is poised to become increasingly important in real-world applications.

Machine learning models often struggle with data points that lie outside their expected range, which can lead to subpar performance. To address this issue, we've developed a new, efficient method called RECol that can identify these unusual data points. RECol works by calculating the reconstruction error for each data point and then uses a threshold to flag those that appear out of the ordinary. Our method has been tested on various datasets and has been found to be highly effective in identifying these data points.

This paper's main objective is to investigate non-linear rough differential equations and their associated control mechanisms, where the control is influenced by a non-linear function of the solution itself, driven by a general $\alpha$-rough path with $\alpha > 1/2$. By establishing the existence and uniqueness of such equations, the research demonstrates that the solution exhibits enhanced regularity compared to traditional rough differential equations, specifically $C(\alpha\alpha)$ regularity. This breakthrough is leveraged to solve stochastic differential equations with non-Lipschitz coefficients, including those driven by a Brownian motion, and shows that the resulting solutions possess a higher regularity of $C(3\alpha\alpha)$, a significant improvement over existing results.

A novel approach to measure neutrino properties involves using the interaction between neutrinos and electromagnetic fields in the presence of strong external fields. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated by analyzing neutrinos passing through the magnetic fields of distant stars and supernovae. The interaction between neutrinos and electromagnetic fields is described by the Lagrangian, which includes a term representing the neutrino's magnetic susceptibility. The effect of this interaction on neutrino propagation is calculated using the density matrix formalism, and the resulting changes in neutrino polarization are analyzed. The study shows that the interaction between neutrinos and electromagnetic fields can lead to the generation of neutrino magnetic moments and other effects, and the magnitude of these effects depends on the strength of the external fields and the distance traveled by the neutrinos. The study also provides estimates of the sensitivity of the method to the neutrino's magnetic susceptibility and the resulting implications for the study of neutrino properties.

The brain's intricate network of neurons and glial cells plays a vital role in its information processing capabilities. In this study, we develop a mean field model to simulate the behavior of this complex system, taking into account the dynamic interactions between the two cell types. Our model reveals that the system can exhibit spontaneous oscillations, which arise from the inherent asymmetry between the two cell types. We further explore the conditions under which these oscillations occur and find that they are influenced by the strength of the connections between the cell types. Our results provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms that drive brain activity and may help to shed light on the causes of neurological disorders.

A particle's first passage to a fixed boundary is a well-documented phenomenon, but less understood is what happens when the boundary itself moves. This study explores how the boundary recedes based on the particle's first passage, and finds that this process can be seen as a type of self-organized criticality. This leads to the particle's first passage time having widely varying and unpredictable values. This effect is demonstrated in a model of a protein moving through a cell membrane, where a receptor's movement is influenced by the membrane's expansion.

We introduce a kinetic theory model that accounts for varying entropy and corresponding hydrodynamic equations. A Poisson map connects the hydrodynamics to the best possible entropy kinetic model, achieved through the principle of maximum entropy.

In medical procedures, the presence of artifacts in video feeds can severely compromise the performance of computer vision systems. To address this issue, we investigated the effectiveness of combining multiple computer vision models to enhance their ability to detect and remove artifacts in endoscopic video streams. Our research involved testing various ensemble methods on diverse datasets, including an original collection of artificial artifacts and an external benchmark. Our findings suggest that ensemble models can indeed improve the robustness of object detection systems, particularly in scenarios with limited training data.

The naming convention of variables and classes in software development is a crucial aspect of the code, and it can greatly impact the understanding and maintenance of the system. In this research, we investigate the characteristics of source code identifiers, specifically how they are named and structured, and how these aspects affect the meaning of the code. We examine a large dataset of Java identifiers, and we analyze their distribution, naming patterns, and semantic relationships. Our findings suggest that the distribution of identifier lengths follows a power law, and that the naming patterns of certain characters are influenced by their meaning. We also identify and analyze the most commonly used naming conventions, and we investigate their impact on the code's semantics. Our research has significant implications for the development of automated tools that can improve the quality of code, such as code completion systems and refactoring tools.

This article outlines a method to construct a specific type of module, known as $\square_q$-module, based on a $q$-shuffle algebra for affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. The module is infinite-dimensional and is characterized by a unique highest weight vector. The construction utilizes a specific basis, known as the Demazure subalgebra basis, to derive an expression for its generating function.

The study of grain growth in polycrystalline materials is a crucial area of research, as it has significant implications for the material's microstructure and properties. This research focuses on grain growth in duplex and triplex systems, using a combination of theoretical and computational methods to investigate the underlying mechanisms. By analyzing the grain-boundary mobility and curvature, the study reveals the complex interactions between grains of different sizes and how they affect the overall grain growth process. The results show that the growth of smaller grains is influenced by the larger grains' mobility and curvature, and that the overall grain growth rate is determined by the size distribution of the grains. The study also provides insights into the formation of triplex systems and their potential applications in materials science.

Recent breakthroughs in 3D human pose and shape estimation have been achieved, but the majority of research has been confined to controlled settings. Consequently, the performance of these methods in real-world scenarios remains uncertain. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new benchmark that replicates real-world conditions and assesses the capabilities of state-of-the-art algorithms in these environments. Our analysis reveals that current methods excel in controlled settings but struggle to generalize to real-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we introduce a new approach that leverages a generative model to create a more realistic training dataset. Our results demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the performance of estimation methods in real-world scenarios.

A novel approach to the superconducting mechanism in dilute systems with localized electrons is proposed. It is demonstrated that a superconducting state can emerge in a dilute system composed of isolated sites with intense electron-electron repulsion, provided the distance between them is sufficiently large. The proposed model is applied to the study of superconducting properties in a specific compound, Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$Fe$_2$As$_2$.

A new approach to combining leptoquark models with the Standard Model is introduced, which enables a unified framework for analyzing their properties. This framework is applicable to both resonant and non-resonant interactions and is versatile enough to accommodate various leptoquark models. It is initially applied to a scalar leptoquark that interacts with a single pair of up- and down-type quarks and corresponding charged leptons, which is then generalized to accommodate more complex interactions.

This study presents a novel sliding-mode control design for a particular class of motion systems, which can be modeled as dynamic systems with uncertain nonlinearities and unknown disturbances. A terminal sliding-mode control approach is employed to develop a robust controller that ensures the system's state converges to the sliding surface in finite time. A key innovation lies in the use of a specific type of sliding surface, which is designed to be more effective in handling real-world motion systems, and which can be proven to be globally asymptotically stable. Furthermore, the control scheme is shown to be insensitive to external disturbances, and a simulation study is presented to validate the controller's performance.

Lithium-ion batteries are widely used in portable electronics and electric vehicles, but their performance is often limited by the rate at which they can be charged and discharged. To address this issue, researchers are exploring ways to optimize the internal structure of these batteries to improve their efficiency. In this study, a new method is proposed that uses ultrasound to measure the physical properties of lithium-ion battery electrodes, which can then be used to design more efficient battery structures. The method relies on a technique called ultrasonic resonance, which measures the speed of sound in the electrode material and provides information about its density and porosity. The results of this study show that this approach can be used to identify the optimal arrangement of battery components and improve their overall performance.

This research proposes a novel approach to designing discrete-time flatness-based controllers for gantry cranes, leveraging fundamental principles to streamline complex controller design. By focusing on the system's nonlinear flat output, the study simplifies the controller design process, enabling the creation of discrete-time flatness-based controllers that can be easily adapted to gantry cranes.

Image captioning models are hindered by the difficulty of generating high-quality captions due to the presence of noise in training data. To overcome this issue, we introduce a novel cooperative distillation method that leverages the collective knowledge of multiple models to refine caption quality. By harnessing the strengths of each model, this approach can effectively mitigate the impact of noisy data and enhance overall performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses the capabilities of individual models in this context.

We investigate the properties of a set of strings $\Sigma^*$, where a set is defined as well-connected if it contains a string for every possible combination of its substrings. We explore well-connected subsets of $\Sigma^*$, denoted as $\mathcal{W}(\Sigma^*)$, and demonstrate that they are closed under the operation of concatenation. Furthermore, we establish that a regular language is contained in $\mathcal{W}(\Sigma^*)$ if and only if it is equivalent to a specific type of language, $R \cdot \Sigma^* \cdot R$, where $R$ is a regular language. We also examine the computational complexity of determining whether a given regular language is contained in $\mathcal{W}(\Sigma^*)$, revealing that this problem is solvable in polynomial time. Additionally, we explore the properties of $\mathcal{W}(\Sigma^*)$ under various operations, including intersection, union, concatenation, and complementation, and show that these operations can be performed in polynomial time.

A category equipped with an ordered structure is analogous to a semigroup with an ordered Green's relation, much like how a semigroup relates to a group. This paper explores the concept of semigroups that respect an inherent order, specifically semigroups of order-preserving transformations. It delves into semigroups that can be embedded within ordered groups and provides a characterization for semigroups that can be embedded within the semigroup of order-preserving transformations. Additionally, it examines semiconfluent semigroups and proves that they can be embedded within semigroups that respect an inherent order.

The depth and width of neural networks significantly impact their performance, and understanding their interplay is crucial for designing effective models. We investigate the relationship between network depth and width in the context of the transformer architecture, specifically focusing on its self-attention mechanism. Our research reveals that the inherent inductive bias of the transformer's self-attention mechanism is closely linked to the depth of the network. We demonstrate that the transformer's self-attention mechanism can be viewed as a form of graph convolution, where the depth of the network determines the effective radius of the graph. This insight allows us to analyze the transformer's performance in terms of its ability to capture information from distant nodes, and to understand how its performance is affected by the width of the network. Our experiments show that the transformer's performance is closely related to the width of the network, and that its ability to capture long-range dependencies is limited by the width of the network. Our research provides a new perspective on the relationship between network depth and width in neural networks, and to the self-attention mechanism in the transformer architecture.

In a simplified model, the masses of the bottom quark and the tau lepton are calculated by considering their respective wave functions and the distribution of the quark and lepton mass in these functions. The resulting masses are found to be 4.4 GeV for the bottom quark and 1.7 GeV for the tau lepton.

Reconstructing three-dimensional models of everyday items held in hands offers a
significant challenge in three-dimensional reconstruction. This paper introduces
a novel method for accurately capturing the geometry of these objects by
leveraging the inherent rigidity of hands. Our approach involves a two-stage
process: initially, hands are reconstructed from a single image using a
pre-trained neural network, and then, the position of the held items is
estimated through a novel optimization technique that incorporates hand
rigidity. Our method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing
methods in multiple evaluation metrics.

The Sun's magnetic field is a significant factor in the Earth's climate system, and its variations are often measured through the Ca II K index. This study aims to create a long-term Ca-K index dataset spanning over a century, utilizing the Kodaikanal Observatory's unique photographic records. By developing a novel method to quantify the index from these images, the researchers have successfully produced a century-long time series. This dataset has been compared with modern Ca-K index measurements, revealing a strong correlation between the two. The study also highlights the potential of this new method for analyzing historical solar data and its implications for understanding the Sun's impact on Earth's climate.

The LHCb experiment has conducted a comprehensive study of the rare decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ using data from 3.03 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions, collected between 2010 and 2012. The analysis utilized a likelihood fit to determine the branching fraction of this decay, which was found to be $(1.95 \pm 0.70 \pm 0.10) \times 10^{-8}$, where the first error is statistical and the second is systematic. This result is in line with the Standard Model prediction, and a further examination of the decay's invariant mass distribution revealed no evidence of intermediate resonances.

A novel approach to distributed symbolic execution has been developed, utilizing a metric derived from test coverage to divide a program into sections for efficient parallel analysis. This innovative technique, called test-depth partitioning, has been implemented within the S2E infrastructure, a flexible platform for constructing execution environments that can be applied to various symbolic execution strategies. Experimental results demonstrate that test-depth partitioning outperforms random partitioning in achieving higher test coverage within a specified time frame.

The relaxation of the magnetization of a system of interacting particles is investigated, with the particles' magnetic moments arranged in a regular pattern. The study reveals that the relaxation of the magnetization is significantly influenced by the initial magnetization state and the particles' magnetic properties. The relaxation process is found to be a two-stage process, with the initial stage characterized by a rapid change in the magnetization and the subsequent stage by a gradual change. The study also shows that the relaxation process can be controlled by adjusting the particles' magnetic properties and the initial magnetization state.

In the realm of machine learning, federated learning stands out as a privacy-preserving method that allows for training on decentralized datasets. However, existing federated learning methods rely on a central server to facilitate communication, which can be impractical in certain social networks. This paper introduces a novel approach called FedSSN, which enables machine learning on decentralized datasets within social networks that only have one-sided trust relationships. By leveraging the concept of trust, FedSSN facilitates the sharing of machine learning models among users, thereby enabling collaborative learning. The proposed method is evaluated using real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving high learning accuracy while maintaining data privacy.

The rapid growth of online social media platforms has led to an explosion of short-text data, which has created a pressing need for effective classification methods. This study investigates the potential of applying recurrent and convolutional neural networks to sequential classification tasks, where texts are generated in a time-dependent order. By incorporating a novel approach that accounts for temporal dependencies, we develop a model that outperforms existing methods on a diverse range of real-world datasets. Our research demonstrates the value of sequential modeling in short-text classification and provides a comprehensive evaluation of the benefits of incorporating temporal information.

A new analytical approach to the study of telecentric Fabry-Pérot etalons has been developed, which takes into account the varying optical path lengths of incoming light beams. This approach, which utilizes a geometric optics framework, is more accurate than previous methods that relied on a single optical path length. The resulting analytical model can be used to predict the spectral response of the etalon, which can then be compared to experimental results. The model's validity has been confirmed through numerical simulations, which have shown that it provides a good approximation of the etalon's behavior, even for high finesse devices.

A compatible matching in a complete bipartite graph is defined as a set of edges that do not conflict with any given precoloring of the vertices. Specifically, a matching is compatible with a precoloring if it can be found by swapping a subset of the precolored edges. This concept leads to a characterization of edge precolored complete bipartite graphs where a specific matching exists, as well as an investigation of the associated computational problem.

The chiplet technology is poised to revolutionize the semiconductor industry, offering a promising solution to the challenges posed by chip manufacturing and design. This revolutionary approach enables the integration of multiple, heterogeneous components onto a single substrate, significantly reducing costs and expediting time-to-market. As a result, chiplet-based systems are well-suited to address the demands of emerging applications, such as AI and machine learning, by facilitating seamless integration of diverse hardware elements. This article delves into the chiplet paradigm, highlighting its benefits and potential applications, and introduces the codelet model, a cutting-edge framework that leverages the capabilities of modern chiplet-based systems to optimize the performance of computationally intensive tasks.

A semiparametric mixture cure model is used to analyze survival data with a cure fraction, where a parametric component models the relationship between a covariate and the probability of being cured, while a nonparametric component models the conditional survival distribution for uncured individuals. We introduce a presmoothing approach to estimate the parameters of this model, which involves a two-stage process. The first stage estimates the probability of being cured using a Cox regression model, and the second stage estimates the remaining parameters using a weighted likelihood function. We show that the proposed estimators have desirable statistical properties, including consistency and asymptotic normality. The performance of the proposed approach is evaluated through simulation studies and a real-world application to a dataset from a clinical trial.

The concept of nonlocal metric dimension was introduced by Khachataryan et al. in 2020. This paper explores the nonlocal metric dimension of various graphs, demonstrating that for any integer k greater than or equal to one, there exist infinitely many graphs with the following properties: (1) the nonlocal metric dimension is equal to k; (2) the ordinary metric dimension is k plus one; and (3) the local metric dimension is also k plus one.

In-memory computing (IMC) offers a promising solution to overcome the limitations of traditional computing systems. However, IMC technology also presents a new security challenge, as it can be exploited to gain unauthorized access to sensitive data. This paper investigates the vulnerabilities of IMC systems to side-channel attacks, specifically focusing on data stored in processing-in-memory (PIM) devices. By examining the memory access patterns of IMC systems, we demonstrate that sensitive data can be compromised through side-channel attacks. Our research highlights the need for further study on the security of IMC systems and emphasizes the importance of addressing this emerging threat.

A new family of polarization kernels is presented, which are derived from shortened versions of the MDS erasure-resilient kernels. These shortened kernels are obtained by removing specific columns from the generator matrix of a Reed-Solomon code. The resulting polarization effect is quantified by the channel parameters of the erasure channel, which are then used to establish a new bound on the polarization rate. This rate is shown to be at least the capacity of the erasure channel, with the bound being achieved at the limit of infinite code length. Additionally, the results are extended to include the binary erasure channel, and a new family of polarization curves is presented, which can be used to determine the required number of erasures to ensure a specific level of error-free decoding.

Seismic data often contains noise that can be challenging to remove, particularly when it's not easily identifiable. Traditional methods for seismic denoising rely on assumptions about the data, such as periodicity or sparsity, which may not hold in all cases. This paper introduces a new approach to seismic denoising that uses a deep neural network to learn patterns from a large dataset of seismic images, allowing it to effectively remove noise from unseen data. By training the network on a large dataset of images, it can then be applied to new data with minimal additional training. This approach, known as transfer learning, has been successfully tested on a range of seismic datasets and has been found to be more effective than traditional methods in some cases.

Researchers have developed a new approach to causal mediation analysis that can handle treatments with varying intensities. This approach addresses the limitations of existing methods by incorporating a continuous variable for treatment intensity and a flexible model for its impact. A novel estimator is proposed, utilizing a double machine learning technique to efficiently estimate the causal effects of the treatment on both the outcome and mediator variables. This approach is demonstrated to be robust against model misspecification and bias, and its effectiveness is showcased through simulation studies and a real-world application involving the impact of a health intervention on patient outcomes.

The papers in this issue cover various aspects of starshades, including theoretical studies, observational data, and technological developments. The issue concludes with a list of key takeaways and a statement of the starshade community's commitment to advancing exoplanet research.

A significant challenge in identifying suicidal tendencies in online communication is the scarcity of annotated data. To address this, we've developed Robin, a large-scale, annotated dataset comprising 100,000 tweets and 10,000 labels. Our analysis reveals that Robin's comprehensive scope and continuous updates make it a valuable resource for research, and its continuous annotation process ensures that the data remains current and relevant.

A novel mechanical model, Schwarzian mechanics, has been developed by extending the principles of reparametrization invariant mechanics. This new theory is fully supersymmetric and its equations of motion are characterized by the Lagrangian's Schwarzian derivative. It is found that the Lagrangian's Schwarzian derivative is itself a symmetry generator. Furthermore, the supersymmetric Schwarzian mechanics can be linearized, resulting in a superparticle model that is fully supersymmetric and reparametrization invariant.

By applying a specific transformation to the metric, we find that the resulting black hole solutions can be obtained for a broad range of nonlinear models, which exhibit varying degrees of deviation from the standard Reissner-Nordstrom solution. The nature of the black hole's non-singularity is heavily influenced by the specific nonlinear model chosen, resulting in distinct spacetime geometries.

Theoretically, it's expected that a paramagnet should transition to a ferromagnet more quickly as the initial temperature increases. However, our Monte Carlo simulations of the Ising model on a square lattice show a contrasting outcome. The simulations reveal that lower initial temperatures actually result in a faster transition to a ferromagnetic state. This counterintuitive result is attributed to the formation of smaller, more easily organized initial clusters at lower temperatures.

We investigate the localization of pairs in one-dimensional quasicrystals with a non-standard power-law hopping mechanism. Our analysis reveals that the motion of these pairs exhibits localization when the quasicrystal's potential is sufficiently strong, with the decay rate of this localization being slower than an exponential function.

This primer provides an overview of multilingual task-oriented dialogue systems, 
a rapidly evolving field in natural language processing. We examine the key 
challenges in building these systems, including handling diverse languages and 
user intent, and discuss potential solutions. We also discuss the limitations 
of existing systems and the necessary steps to overcome them. Our primer aims 
to be a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners working on 
multilingual dialogue systems.

The splicing process is a crucial mechanism for generating diverse proteins from a single gene, but it is also a highly regulated process that can be influenced by various factors. In this study, we investigate the relationship between splicing regulation and gene expression levels in human cells, specifically by examining the differential expression of exons and genes. We found that genes with higher expression levels tend to have more regulated alternative splicing, but the correlation between splicing and expression levels is not consistent across all genes. Furthermore, we found that genes with similar splicing levels can have different expression levels, suggesting that splicing regulation is not a direct result of gene expression. To better understand the mechanisms of splicing regulation, we analyzed the patterns of splicing in different genes and identified two distinct modes of regulation: one that is correlated with gene expression levels and one that is not. Our findings suggest that splicing regulation is a complex process that can be influenced by multiple factors, including gene expression levels.

The increasing importance of data privacy has led to the implementation of various regulations worldwide, with GDPR being a notable example. These regulations require organizations to implement technical measures to safeguard data, but the exact nature of these measures is often unclear. This study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining how organizations interpret and implement technical measures in their compliance processes. Through a qualitative study involving 20 interviews with data protection professionals, the research highlights the challenges faced by organizations in translating technical measures into practical actions. It also identifies the key factors influencing these challenges, such as data protection policies, organizational structures, and the complexity of data protection tasks. The findings provide valuable insights into the implementation of technical measures and offer practical recommendations for organizations seeking to improve their data protection practices.

We've compared our results to a theoretical model that incorporates the effects of initial-state parton scattering and final-state parton interactions, and found that the model accurately reproduces the observed features of the correlation function.

The presence of atmospheres on rocky exoplanets is crucial for understanding their characteristics and potential habitability. This research focuses on the current state of knowledge regarding the atmospheres of rocky exoplanets, particularly those with an Earth-like mass. We examine the available data on the atmospheres of rocky exoplanets, including those with a mass similar to that of our planet, and discuss the most effective methods for detecting and analyzing their atmospheres. We also explore the most probable compositions of these atmospheres, taking into account the effects of stellar radiation and the planet's surface, and consider the implications of their composition for the planet's habitability.

A graph G is called k-disjunct if the set of its k-colorings in any k-coloring graph has no common neighbors.  A circulant graph D is called dispersible if the underlying graph G is k-colorable for every k greater than or equal to the maximum degree of D. In this paper, we show that for n being a multiple of 4, the graph D is dispersible for all but a finite number of pairs (d, r).  Additionally, we demonstrate that the graph D is dispersible for all but a finite number of odd values of n, where d is equal to the square root of n, and r is equal to the floor of the square root of n.

The inverse of a matrix is a fundamental concept in linear algebra, with applications spanning various fields such as machine learning, statistics, and signal processing. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in developing efficient algorithms for matrix inversion, particularly for large matrices. This research focuses on enhancing the performance of iterative matrix inversion methods by employing higher-order Newton-like techniques and optimizing their implementation on GPUs. We introduce a novel approach, the Multiple Multiple Correction (MMC) method, which generalizes existing methods and accelerates convergence by incorporating higher-order corrections. The proposed generalization of theMMC method is then adapted for GPU acceleration, leveraging the fast convergence properties of the methods and a divide-and-conquer strategy to optimize the inversion process. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in accelerating the convergence of iterative matrix inversion algorithms.

We examine the impact of the slow-roll parameter's time derivative on primordial perturbations, particularly focusing on the back reaction of these perturbations on the background evolution. We derive the primordial power spectrum of curvature perturbations, incorporating the back reaction's influence, and investigate how the power spectrum is affected by the time derivative of the slow-roll parameter. We find that the power spectrum is suppressed when the time derivative of the slow-roll parameter is positive, and enhanced when it is negative. We also consider the case of ultra-slow-roll inflation, where the time derivative of the slow-roll parameter is positive, and the amplitude of primordial power spectrum is suppressed by the back reaction. We calculate the primordial power spectrum for the model of ultra-slow-roll inflation, which is motivated by the potential for a large field inflation, and find that the suppression of the power spectrum is significant. We discuss the implications of our results for the primordial power spectrum, and the role of the back reaction in determining the power spectrum.

In the context of assortment optimization, we examine a scenario where customers have M different types, each with distinct purchase probabilities for products in a given set. The goal is to determine which products to offer to each customer type in order to maximize revenue. We develop a polynomial-time algorithm to solve this optimization problem, thereby providing a first-time efficient solution to a previously unresolved challenge.

This article presents a novel statistical approach to survival analysis and
comparative event rate analysis, which can be seen as an extension of the
traditional case-control methodology. The proposed method, called "calibration
of survival," utilizes a casebase, a subset of the full dataset, to estimate
hazard rates and derive key parameters. The method's efficacy is demonstrated
through the construction of a casebase from a subset of the well-known
Stanford heart transplant dataset, yielding comparable results to a full model.
The approach's flexibility is further demonstrated by its ability to incorporate
covariate adjustments, resulting in more accurate estimates. The method's
versatility is also showcased through its application to a larger dataset,
yielding similar results to a full model, albeit with reduced computational
cost. The proposed method's utility is further illustrated through its ability
to generate a calibration curve, providing a visual representation of
survival estimates. The article concludes by highlighting the method's
potential for use in a wide range of settings, including situations where
full models are infeasible due to computational constraints or data
limitations.

The application of differential equations in solving multi-loop, multi-scale Feynman integrals has been highly effective in recent years. This article provides an overview of the differential equation method, highlighting its key features and applications, and discusses the latest developments in the field.

The Object Data Storage (ODS) approach is a relatively new method for storing data, characterized by the storage of both data and metadata in the same I/O buffer. This approach has the potential to significantly enhance performance by reducing I/O operations and improving data access efficiency. This paper compares the performance of a custom-built ODS plugin for Lustre, a widely used distributed file system, with a direct comparison to Data Admission Virtual File System (DAVS) using native ODS features. Performance tests were conducted using the STREAM and I/O benchmarking tools, and the results indicate that the custom ODS plugin outperforms DAVS in read and write operations.

This research introduces an online admission control system for electric vehicles at public parking facilities. The proposed method aims to maximize revenue by accepting a subset of electric vehicles, taking into consideration the parking fees and the costs associated with finding parking. The parking facility's objective is to optimize its overall revenue. The study presents an optimal solution to the admission control problem, which is proven to be the best possible. The results show that the proposed solution achieves a 1/2 competitive ratio. The study also extends its findings to a more complex scenario where parking fees vary based on the time of day. The proposed solution is proven to be the most effective for this scenario as well. The study further explores the impact of limited parking availability on the optimal solution, which is proven to be the most effective for this scenario as well. The study also considers the impact of limited parking availability on the optimal solution, which is proven to be the most effective for this scenario as well.

Furthermore, we provide a method for constructing such linear codes over finite fields, and we also examine the existence of a specific type of linear code with a particular characteristic over finite fields.

The transition to a low-carbon energy system is crucial for achieving climate goals, but it also poses challenges for land use and water resources. This study examines the trade-offs between land use and the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector in the American West. We analyzed the potential for carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide emissions to be offset by reforestation and the associated land use requirements. Our results indicate that reforestation could effectively mitigate emissions from the power sector, but it would require a significant increase in forested area. This research highlights the importance of considering land use trade-offs in the development of low-carbon energy systems and the need for a comprehensive approach that balances land use and emissions reduction.

In randomized trials, the impact of a treatment is often evaluated by comparing outcomes between those who received it and those who did not. However, this comparison is frequently complicated by the presence of unobserved confounding factors, particularly in studies involving cluster-randomization. A key challenge arises when the treatment effect is influenced by unmeasured characteristics of the clusters, such as their inherent properties or the treatment assignment process. To address this issue, we propose a framework that distinguishes between different types of treatment effects, including the average effect, the average treatment effect on the treated, and the local average treatment effect. This framework is particularly useful in studies involving cluster-randomization, where it can be used to develop consistent estimators and valid confidence intervals. We illustrate the utility of this approach by applying it to a study of a meningococcal vaccine, where it reveals that the choice of estimand can have a significant impact on the estimated treatment effect.

This study delves into the spectral characteristics of a fracto-Mobius octagonal network, denoted as $FM_8(N,k)$, where $k$ represents the iteration level and $N$ signifies the fractal dimension. $FM_8(N,k)$ is defined as a fractal fracturing of the Mobius octagonal graph $M_8(k)$. We establish the spectral characteristics of $FM_8(N,k)$, including its normalized Laplacian spectrum, eigenvalues, and eigenvectors. Moreover, we explore the relationship between the eigenvalues of $FM_8(N,k)$ and its topological invariants, specifically the Euler characteristic and the first Zagreb index.

In the realm of distributed contextual bandits, a group of learners collaborates with a shared reward function, despite having distinct data sets. The learners' goal is to identify the optimal policy that maximizes the reward by leveraging their individual contexts. This research focuses on a specific scenario where the contexts are not interconnected, and the learners' contexts are linearly related to the unknown parameter of the reward function. The study presents a novel algorithm that enables the learners to achieve a collective regret of O(T^(2/3)) with a linear dependence on the time horizon T, and the algorithm's complexity is O(d^3) in terms of the dimensionality of the contexts. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through a series of experiments.

The creation of large, confidential datasets is a common challenge in machine learning, particularly in healthcare. This research proposes a novel method for generating synthetic electronic health records that can be used to replicate the characteristics of a specific patient population, in this case, individuals with cystic fibrosis. Our dataset is notable for its extensive longitudinal data, encompassing 127 variables and 1,252 time-stamped entries per patient. We evaluated the effectiveness of our approach using a combination of statistical and machine learning-based metrics, and found that the synthetic data closely mirrors the original dataset. Moreover, our findings suggest that the generated synthetic data can be used to develop and test machine learning models, and that the data can be used to identify key factors influencing patient outcomes.

Novelpy is an open-source Python package that offers a platform for analyzing
novelty and disruptiveness in scientific and technological data, particularly
bibliometric and patent data. The software's core algorithms are based on
established bibliometric metrics, including the h-index, citation counts, and
other key indicators. The package is designed to be user-friendly and
accessible, with functions that can be easily integrated into existing
workflows. By providing a standardized approach to novelty analysis, Novelpy
enables researchers and professionals to compare and evaluate data across
different domains and fields. The package's open-source nature ensures that it
can be freely accessed and modified by the research community, promoting
collaboration and innovation in the field of bibliometrics and technology
management.

We have developed a method to control the intensity of a probe pulse in space and time by exploiting the cross-phase modulation effect. This technique is demonstrated using a high-energy, femtosecond probe pulse and an intense, carrier-envelope-stabilized pulse. The technique's effectiveness is showcased through both theoretical and experimental results, where a single carrier-envelope-stabilized pulse is used to modulate the temporal intensity of the probe pulse. The technique's versatility is further illustrated by its application to generate a desired spatial intensity distribution on the probe pulse.

The integration of robotics in sports has been explored through the use of robotic equipment, allowing for the examination of human athletic abilities. This study focuses on the application of a robotic system to archery, specifically the National Olympic Recurve discipline. A robotic arm was designed to precisely execute the shooting process, which involves drawing, aiming, and releasing an arrow. A robotic hand was developed to grip and release the string, replicating the movements of a human archer. A robotic arm was then employed to position the bow and arrow, allowing for the investigation of the system's capabilities and limitations. A series of tests were conducted to evaluate the robotic system's ability to shoot arrows with varying degrees of accuracy and consistency. A robotic system was found to be capable of replicating the movements of a human archer, but with some limitations in terms of accuracy and consistency. A robotic system was found to be less accurate than a human archer, but with a higher degree of consistency in its shots. A robotic system was found to be a promising tool for the study of human athletic abilities, but with some limitations in terms of accuracy and consistency.

Cross-domain recommendation systems aim to enhance user experience by expanding the scope of recommendations beyond a single domain. However, conventional methods often rely on a single metric to measure similarity between users and items, which can lead to suboptimal results. To address this limitation, a novel approach called Dual Metric Learning (DuMeL) is introduced, which utilizes two distinct metrics to capture different aspects of user-item interactions. By combining these metrics, DuMeL can provide more accurate and diverse recommendations. To optimize the performance of DuMeL, a novel training method called Dual Ranking is developed, which takes into account the unique properties of each metric. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of DuMeL over existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We examine a reduced set of modal mu-calculus formulas, denoted as MLμ, which excludes the least fixed point operator. We establish that the logical systems of synchronous and asynchronous distributed automata accurately capture exactly the properties definable in MLμ.

A novel method for studying thermal conductivity in two-dimensional complex plasma layers has been developed. This approach involves creating a localized temperature gradient within a plasma layer using a laser, and measuring the resulting thermal flux. This technique has been applied to a plasma layer composed of dielectric microparticles suspended in a two-dimensional layer of a helium-based complex plasma. The thermal conductivity of the plasma layers has been determined for layers with particle concentrations of 0.02 to 0.05 mg/cm^3 and layer thicknesses of 0.1 to 0.5 mm. The experimental results show that thermal conductivity is directly proportional to the particle concentration and inversely proportional to the layer thickness. The experimental findings are in agreement with theoretical predictions based on a model of heat transfer through the plasma layer.

This study explores the properties of linear combinations of vectors from unordered data sets, specifically focusing on their ordering characteristics. Given a set of $n$ real-valued observations $X = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ and a set of $m$ nonnegative weights $w = (w_1, \ldots, w_m)$, the research investigates the ordering of vectors generated by combining $x_i$ and $x_j$ in various ways, where $i$ and $j$ range from $1$ to $n$ and $m$ respectively. The analysis reveals that for certain weight distributions, the ordering of these combinations remains consistent, and provides a general framework for determining this behavior. The research also identifies the conditions under which the ordering of these combinations remains consistent for all possible weight distributions.

A significant challenge in cardio-angiography is the high radiation exposure to the patient, which is typically mitigated by reducing the X-ray beam's frequency. However, this approach is limited by the need to balance image quality and radiation exposure. A novel solution to this problem has been developed using a deep learning-based video interpolation technique, which can generate high-quality video sequences from a limited number of frames. This approach has been successfully implemented using a convolutional neural network, which has been trained on a large dataset of cardio-angiography videos. The results of this study demonstrate that the proposed method can significantly reduce the X-ray beam's frequency while maintaining high image quality. The proposed method has the potential to revolutionize the way cardio-angiography is performed, making it safer and more efficient for both patients and medical professionals.

These measurements will encompass the study of Higgs production, Y(1S) and Y(2S) production, and the exploration of physics beyond the Standard Model. Our research focuses on the ejection of stars from the Galactic Center due to the secular perturbation caused by intermediate-mass companions. We've developed a new method to calculate the ejection rate of stars, which takes into account the complex dynamics of these systems. Our findings indicate that this perturbation mechanism is more effective at ejecting stars than previously thought, with an ejection rate that is significantly higher than that of other mechanisms. We've also discovered that this perturbation mechanism is capable of ejecting stars at a rate that is comparable to that of other mechanisms, with a significant impact on the overall ejection rate. Our research has important implications for our understanding of the Galactic Center and the formation of hypervelocity stars.

A class of multiplicative stochastic differential equations with singular drift is analyzed, where the noise component is defined as the combination of a two-dimensional white noise and a deterministic term. The existence and uniqueness of weak solutions to these stochastic equations are established, with the key finding being that the noise term effectively regularizes the otherwise irregular drift, a phenomenon known as regularization by noise.

Despite the remarkable advancements in NLP, language models still struggle to adapt to novel tasks, particularly when training data is limited. To address this, we've developed a new framework called Adaptor, which enables the efficient adaptation of language models to new domains and tasks. By focusing on domain-specific attributes and task-specific objectives, Adaptor allows for the creation of adaptable language models that can be fine-tuned to specific domains and tasks. Our proposed framework outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, particularly when working with scarce data. Adaptor is available for public use on the HuggingFace platform.

The vast majority of traffic sign detection research has been conducted on European and North American datasets, which are typically characterized by a small number of classes and uniform image quality. However, real-world scenarios involve significantly more diverse traffic signs, including those with varying appearances and quality, as well as language barriers. This paper presents the Mapillary Traffic Sign Dataset, a comprehensive global dataset comprising 1.2 million images of traffic signs, which features 1200 distinct classes and is accompanied by a novel detection and classification benchmark. The accompanying Mapillary Traffic Sign Detector model, which leverages this dataset, is also made available.

Collaborative filtering has been a long-standing challenge in recommender systems,
with many recent studies focusing on self-supervised learning to enhance
recommendations. However, existing methods often rely on a single type of
self-supervised task, which may not fully capture the underlying user-item
relationships. To address this limitation, we propose SelfCF, a new framework
for collaborative filtering that leverages multiple self-supervised tasks to
improve recommendations. Our framework is straightforward to implement and
can be easily integrated with existing collaborative filtering models.
Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that SelfCF
significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with a notable 1.5%
increase in accuracy on one dataset.

This paper investigates the Tevelev degrees of a specific class of maps from a blow-up of the complex projective line to itself, under certain conditions, to gain insight into the enumerative geometry of rational curves. We establish a recursive formula for the Tevelev degree of such maps, which can be applied to any map with a particular type of degree distribution. Additionally, we derive a formula for the Tevelev degree of a map with a specific configuration of target points, which has significant implications for understanding the enumerative geometry of rational curves.

A gapped Dirac semimetal phase featuring a combined linear and parabolic dispersion relation is theoretically examined. This gapped Dirac semimetal phase is characterized by a ground state featuring a single minimum, with a corresponding state at the highest energy level featuring a single maximum. This phase is distinguished from the gapped graphene semimetal phase, which exhibits four maxima and four minima at the highest and lowest energy levels respectively. This theoretical model is applicable to a variety of materials, including those with tetragonal, hexagonal, and cubic crystal structures. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the unique electronic properties of the gapped Dirac semimetal phase, with a particular focus on its topological characteristics.

We examine a semi-stable degeneration of surfaces over a discrete valuation field, focusing on a specific type of fiber product that arises from a given surface $X$ over a field $K$. We prove that the closure of a specific subset of a fiber product $X_k \times_K \overline{K}$ is an algebraic variety, and show that this product is isomorphic to a specific type of compactification of the base field $K$. This result is applied to a specific type of degeneration of abelian varieties, and we demonstrate that the fiber product is isomorphic to a compactification of an abelian variety, and that a specific type of degeneration is equivalent to a specific type of degeneration over a field extension.

The discovery of gravitational waves has been a significant breakthrough in the field of astronomy, but it has been hindered by the limitations of current detectors. These detectors can only detect a small fraction of the gravitational wave population, resulting in a significant loss of information. To overcome this challenge, researchers are working on developing more sensitive detectors that can detect higher-order modes of gravitational waves. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of these new detectors in detecting higher-order modes and assess their potential to improve the detection rate. To achieve this, researchers are using simulated binary black hole signals and analyzing the detectability of higher-order modes using different detector configurations. The results show that future detectors will be able to detect higher-order modes in a significant number of cases, and that the detection of these modes can provide valuable information about the binary black hole system.
